## Why it made the list

Sometimes it’s the practical homes that offer the biggest opportunity. Set on a spacious plot surrounded by the beautiful nature of Gunnarskog, this well-maintained home gives you room to settle into Swedish country life without taking on a long renovation project.

## Is €83,000 a good price for this home?

29 of the 39 homes in Sweden on RealHunt have a lower asking price.

Asking prices are what the seller asks, not what homes sell for. Compare with recent sales in the same village before you make an offer.

## What it costs to buy this home

Buying in Sweden adds about 1.5-3.5% in taxes and fees on top of the price: roughly €1,245 to €2,905 here, so plan for about €84,245 to €85,905 in total.

Stamp duty on the title (lagfart) of 1.5% of the price or tax value, whichever is higher, plus a SEK 825 fee; if you borrow and need new mortgage deeds (pantbrev), 2% of their amount plus a SEK 375 fee; optional legal advice; the seller normally pays the agent, and a cooperative flat (bostadsrätt) has no lagfart.

Every year: Houses pay a municipal property fee (kommunal fastighetsavgift) of SEK 10,425 in 2026, or 0.75% of the tax value if that is lower.

General information, not tax advice: ask a local lawyer or notary for the exact figure.

## Where it is: Gunnarskog

The home is in Gunnarskog, Värmland, Sweden.

There is a lake 4 km away (Lill-Mörttjärnet); the nearest airport is about 45 km away (Torsby Airport (TYF)); the nearest shop is about 3 km away; the nearest train station is about 13 km away (Åmotfors). Distances are in a straight line.

## Why it made the list

A fully renovated 215 m² loft on the top floor of a historic building, below the Larzac plateau. The cathedral living room is over 82 m² with exposed timber beams, light from both sides and a pellet stove. Five bedrooms including a master suite, a 12 m² kitchen and a 31 m² terrace with panoramic views over the Lergue. Energy class B. Asking €285,000, about €1,326/m².

## Is €285,000 a good price for this home?

At about €1,326 per m², this home is 13% above the median for France on RealHunt (€1,175 per m², across 48 homes checked by a person). 17 of those homes cost more per m².

Asking prices are what the seller asks, not what homes sell for. Compare with recent sales in the same village before you make an offer.

## What it costs to buy this home

Buying in France adds about 7-8.5% in taxes and fees on top of the price: roughly €19,950 to €24,225 here, so plan for about €304,950 to €309,225 in total.

Transfer taxes (droits de mutation) of about 5.8%, or about 6.3% in departments that raised their rate for 2025 to March 2028; notary fee (émoluments) on a sliding scale from 3.87% down to 0.799% plus 20% VAT, about 1.3% on a €150,000 home; land security contribution (contribution de sécurité immobilière) 0.10%; disbursements (débours) of about €800 to €1,200; the agent fee is usually built into the advertised price (FAI) and paid by the seller, sometimes shared.

Every year: Owners pay an annual property tax (taxe foncière) set by the local authorities, and owners of a furnished second home also pay housing tax (taxe d'habitation), which some communes raise by a surcharge of 5% to 60%.

General information, not tax advice: ask a local lawyer or notary for the exact figure.
